chunks: "The differential equation for an inductor is v equals L di over dt : the voltage across it is the inductance times the rate of change of current through it, with current flowing into the plus terminal.
You can also flip it around into integral form: the current is the initial current plus one over L times the integral of the voltage, i(t) equals i(t 0) plus 1 over L the integral of v dt .
I find that form more intuitive.
It says the inductor current is the running total of the voltage you've applied, so if you put a constant voltage across it, the current ramps linearly at V over L amps per second.
A few things fall out of it. If the current is constant, the voltage is zero, so at DC an ideal inductor is a short.
The current can't jump instantly, because that would need infinite di/dt and therefore infinite voltage; that's the continuity condition.
And if you try to interrupt the current fast, you get a big voltage spike. A practical example is a buck converter.
When the switch is on, the inductor sees V in minus V out and the current ramps up; when it's off, it sees -V out and ramps down.
In steady state the up-ramp and down-ramp must cancel, so the average inductor voltage is zero. That's volt-second balance, and it's how you derive V out equals D times V in ."
